body:
A battery installation is more than a collection of cells

A single electrochemical cell stores a limited quantity of energy. Larger installations combine many cells and add equipment that controls charging, discharging, temperature, protection and connection to the electricity network.

A Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) is the complete arrangement used to store electrical energy in batteries and deliver it later. BESS installations can serve homes, commercial buildings, industries, renewable-energy plants, substations and large electricity grids.

Cells, modules, packs and racks

Cells can be grouped into modules, modules into larger packs or racks, and these assemblies into a complete storage system. The exact arrangement varies among manufacturers and applications. Some systems use cells directly in larger structural assemblies without following every intermediate grouping.

The terms cell, module and BESS therefore refer to different levels. A cell is the basic electrochemical unit; a BESS also includes the equipment needed to operate that unit safely and usefully at the intended scale.

Important components of a grid-scale BESS

ComponentMain purpose
Battery cells and assembliesStore energy through electrochemical reactions
Battery Management System (BMS)Monitors battery conditions and enforces protective operating limits
Power Conversion System (PCS)Converts electricity between the battery's direct-current form and the alternating-current form used by the grid
Energy Management System (EMS)Coordinates charging and discharging according to operating requirements
Thermal managementHelps keep cells within suitable temperature limits
Protection and safety equipmentDetects faults, isolates affected equipment and supports emergency response
Transformer and switchgearConnect and protect the system at the required network level

BMS and EMS are not interchangeable

The BMS concentrates on battery condition and protection. It monitors quantities such as cell voltage, temperature and estimates of state of charge. It may limit or interrupt operation when conditions become unsafe.

The EMS manages the wider operating objective: for example, charging during a period of surplus solar generation and discharging during the evening peak. An EMS must respect limits communicated by the BMS.

The PCS is different again. It performs the electrical conversion needed for charging and discharging. Because batteries charge and discharge using direct current, a grid-connected BESS needs suitable conversion equipment to exchange power with an alternating-current network.

Charging and discharging do not require an attached solar plant

A battery located beside a solar plant may charge from that plant. But a BESS can also charge from the grid or another permitted electricity source. The term battery storage describes the storage technology, not the original source of the energy.

Consider 3 applications:

  • Household solar storage: electricity generated during daylight can be stored for later household use.
  • Industrial backup: stored electricity can support selected loads when the normal supply is interrupted, subject to system configuration.
  • Grid-scale storage: a utility installation can charge during low-demand or high-generation periods and discharge when the network requires support.

A stationary BESS can also help supply fast power adjustments, reduce short peaks in demand and support a microgrid. The services actually available depend on its power rating, energy capacity, controls and remaining stored energy.

A BESS with a high power rating may respond quickly but still have limited discharge duration. Conversely, a battery with substantial energy capacity cannot necessarily deliver all that energy at an arbitrarily high power.

Prelims focus

  • A cell is the basic electrochemical unit; a BESS is a complete storage installation.
  • BMS monitors and protects battery operation.
  • PCS performs electrical power conversion.
  • EMS coordinates when and how the storage system operates.
  • Grid batteries can charge from sources other than solar panels.
  • Trap: BMS and EMS have related but different functions.

[U.S. Department of Energy, Battery Energy Storage Systems: Considerations for Implementation, 5 August 2025, slides 8–10 and 13–15; U.S. Department of Energy, Lithium-ion Batteries: Technology Strategy Assessment, July 2023, Lithium-ion Deployment and Design, printed p. 2; Ministry of Power, National Framework for Promoting Energy Storage Systems, August 2023, Section 4, p. 3; sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

body:
Why battery operation requires safety controls

Rechargeable batteries store useful energy in a compact form. If a cell is damaged or operated outside suitable limits, unwanted chemical and electrical reactions may release energy rapidly. The risk depends on the cell chemistry, its physical construction, operating conditions and the protective systems around it.

Important hazards include internal short circuits, external short circuits, overcharging, excessive temperatures, physical damage and the spread of a fault from one cell to neighbouring cells.

Thermal runaway

Thermal runaway is an uncontrolled self-heating process in which heat generated by reactions inside a cell causes further heating and increasingly rapid reactions. In a severe lithium-ion battery incident, the cell may release hot gases, including flammable and hazardous substances. Ignition or gas accumulation can cause a fire or explosion hazard.

Thermal runaway is not the same as every instance of ordinary battery warming. Some heating occurs during normal operation. The dangerous condition arises when internal heat-producing reactions become self-sustaining and are no longer adequately controlled.

Battery protection may include cell monitoring, limits on charging and discharging, thermal management, protective separation between cells, fault isolation and fire or gas detection. The purpose is both to reduce the probability of a fault and to limit its consequences.

LFP cells generally offer better thermal stability than many high-energy nickel-rich lithium-ion variants, but better thermal stability does not mean zero fire risk. Proper system-level protection remains necessary.

Why batteries lose capacity

Battery degradation means a gradual reduction in performance over time or with use. Two important forms are calendar ageing and cycle ageing.

  • Calendar ageing: gradual chemical changes that occur with the passage of time, even when the battery is not being cycled frequently. Temperature and storage conditions influence this process.
  • Cycle ageing: changes associated with repeated charging and discharging. The amount of cycling, charging conditions and operating limits affect the rate of deterioration.

Repeated exposure to high temperatures, unsuitable charging conditions or severe operating demands can accelerate ageing. Deep discharge, prolonged storage at certain high states of charge and rapid charging under unfavourable conditions may also increase degradation, depending on the cell chemistry and controls.

Ageing may reduce the amount of usable energy or increase internal resistance. These changes can affect both discharge duration and the power that can be delivered under specified conditions.

State of charge and state of health

State of charge (SOC) estimates how much charge remains relative to a defined capacity. State of health (SOH) describes how the battery's present condition compares with a reference condition, commonly a new battery's capacity or resistance.

A battery can have a state of charge of 100% and still have less usable energy than it had when new. Full charge is not the same as full original capacity.

What happens when a battery reaches the end of its first use?

End of useful life for one application does not always mean that every cell has lost all capacity. After appropriate safety and performance assessment, some batteries may be refurbished or used in a less demanding application. Others need material recovery.

Reuse is not automatic. Damaged or deteriorated cells can present safety risks, and the remaining condition must be assessed before another application is considered.

Battery recycling

Recycling aims to recover valuable materials and reduce the environmental burden of discarded batteries. Depending on the battery chemistry and recycling process, recoverable substances may include lithium, nickel, cobalt, copper, aluminium or lead.

Common lithium-ion recycling approaches include mechanical separation, high-temperature processing and chemical recovery.

  • Mechanical processing: batteries or components are safely prepared and separated into material streams. A mixture containing electrode materials is often called black mass.
  • Pyrometallurgy: high-temperature treatment is used to recover selected metals or produce intermediate materials for further processing.
  • Hydrometallurgy: chemical solutions are used to separate and recover selected materials.

The materials recovered and the efficiency of recovery differ among facilities. Recycling should not be understood as automatically recovering every constituent of a battery without loss.

Battery waste management in India

India's Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 were published on 24 August 2022. They cover portable, automotive, electric-vehicle and industrial batteries, including different battery chemistries.

The rules are based on Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR). Under this principle, battery producers, including importers, have obligations relating to the collection and environmentally sound recycling or refurbishment of waste batteries. The framework provides for registration, reporting and certificates associated with recycling or refurbishment.

Waste batteries must enter appropriate collection and processing channels rather than being discarded with ordinary waste. The rules prohibit their disposal through landfilling or incineration. India also notified amendments after 2022; the amendment dated 24 February 2025 addressed labelling of EPR registration numbers.

The 2022 rules established the battery-waste framework; the 2025 amendment did not establish EPR for the first time. These dates and legal provisions are stated for the content cutoff of 16 November 2026.

Prelims focus

  • Thermal runaway is uncontrolled, self-sustaining heating inside a cell.
  • Calendar ageing occurs with time; cycle ageing is linked to charging and discharging.
  • SOC indicates remaining charge; SOH indicates the battery's condition relative to a reference.
  • Black mass is a battery-recycling material stream containing electrode materials.
  • India's Battery Waste Management Rules were published on 24 August 2022.
  • Trap: A fully charged aged battery need not have its original energy capacity.

[U.S. Department of Energy, Energy Storage Safety Strategic Plan, May 2024, Sections 5.2 and 5.3, concerning cell hazards and safety controls; U.S. Department of Energy, Lithium-ion Batteries: Technology Strategy Assessment, July 2023, Lithium-ion Deployment and Design and Advanced Controls, printed pp. 2 and 8; U.S. Department of Energy, Alternative Fuels Data Center, Batteries for Electric Vehicles, battery recycling section; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Battery Waste Management Rules, notification published 24 August 2022; Press Information Bureau, Government of India, Government Notifies Battery Waste Management Rules, 25 August 2022; Press Information Bureau, Circular Economy for Batteries, 21 August 2025; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Rules and Regulations, Battery Waste Management Amendment Rules, notification dated 24 February 2025; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

body:
The basic idea

Pumped-storage hydropower is a method of storing energy by moving water between 2 reservoirs at different elevations. Electricity is used to lift water from a lower reservoir to an upper reservoir. When electricity is required, water is released downhill through a turbine, which drives a generator.

The important feature is that the plant can operate in both directions: it consumes electricity while pumping and produces electricity while generating.

Because water can be moved repeatedly between the reservoirs, pumped storage is sometimes described as a water battery. This is an analogy. The plant stores gravitational potential energy, not electrochemical energy.

The 2 operating modes

Pumping mode

During periods of low electricity demand or surplus generation, the plant uses electricity to operate pumps. Water is transferred from the lower reservoir to the upper reservoir. The stored energy increases because the water has been raised against gravity.

Generating mode

During periods when electricity is needed, water flows from the upper reservoir towards the lower reservoir. Its gravitational potential energy is converted into the kinetic energy of moving water, then into mechanical energy at the turbine, and finally into electricity at the generator.

Many pumped-storage plants use reversible pump-turbine units, although arrangements with separate pumps and turbines are also possible. The operating principle does not depend on every installation having the same machine arrangement.

Why the height difference matters

The energy stored when water is raised depends on its mass and the vertical height through which it is lifted. The elementary expression for gravitational potential energy is:

Potential energy = mass × gravitational acceleration × height.

This can be written as E = mgh, where m is mass, g is gravitational acceleration and h is vertical height difference.

For the same mass of water, a greater elevation difference gives more gravitational potential energy. For the same elevation difference, moving more water increases stored energy. The effective operating head and usable reservoir volume therefore matter when assessing a pumped-storage site.

The head is the difference in water level relevant to the movement of water through the plant. It is not simply the height of a dam wall.

Pumped storage versus ordinary hydropower

A conventional reservoir hydropower station commonly generates electricity using water collected from natural inflows. A pumped-storage station additionally uses electricity to return water to a higher level for later generation.

A hydropower plant does not become a functioning pumped-storage plant merely because it has a reservoir or reversible machinery. It must be capable of performing the pumping operation in practice.

Conventional reservoir hydropower: uses stored water and natural inflows to generate electricity. Pumped storage: also consumes electricity to pump water uphill for later generation.

Open-loop and closed-loop pumped storage

Pumped-storage plants may be classified by whether their reservoirs have an ongoing hydrological connection to naturally flowing water.

  • Open-loop: the system remains continuously connected to a natural water body or flowing water feature, such as a river.
  • Closed-loop: the reservoirs are not continuously connected to a naturally flowing water body. Water may still be added initially or periodically to replace losses.

The expressions on-stream and off-stream also appear in project classifications. They describe how a project is situated relative to natural watercourses. They are related to, but should not automatically be treated as perfect substitutes for, the formal open-loop and closed-loop definitions.

Efficiency, duration and environmental considerations

A pumped-storage plant uses more electricity for a complete pumping-and-generation cycle than it returns. Losses occur in pumps, turbines, generators, motors, water passages and associated equipment.

Pumped storage is especially useful when a power system needs substantial energy over several hours. The practical discharge duration depends on the usable water volume, elevation difference, generating capacity and operating restrictions.

Suitable locations require favourable terrain, water availability, reservoir arrangements and a practicable connection to the grid. Project assessment must also consider land, habitat, water use, local communities, sedimentation and the effects of construction or altered water movement. Closed-loop projects may reduce some direct effects on natural aquatic systems but do not eliminate all environmental impacts.

Prelims focus

  • Pumped storage is based on gravitational potential energy.
  • Pumping mode consumes electricity and lifts water to the upper reservoir.
  • Generating mode releases water downhill through a turbine.
  • Stored gravitational energy increases with water mass and elevation difference.
  • Open-loop systems have an ongoing connection to natural water; closed-loop systems do not.
  • Trap: A hydropower station with a reservoir is not necessarily an operational pumped-storage plant.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, Work and Energy, printed pp. 152–155, potential energy and conservation of energy; U.S. Department of Energy, Pumped Storage Hydropower, sections What Is Pumped Storage Hydropower? and Open-Loop Versus Closed-Loop Pumped Storage Hydropower; U.S. Department of Energy, Pumped Storage Hydropower: Technology Strategy Assessment, July 2023, section on technology and operation; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]
